Pierro explains that the Tsaritsa's transcription prisms and Stellar Linchpins carry his power and so are free of some of Teyvat's laws. She records each day's memories in one so that changes to Irminsul cannot touch them.

47.comment: Descender: Stellar Linchpins and the Third Descender
47.content: During the limited-time Sunny Summer Fontinalia event (6.7), Marionette (Sandrone) shared Fatui research: the Gnoses made from the Third Descender's remains consolidate the Archon system, Visions come from that same system and so are partly linked to him, and when a Stellar Linchpin manifests, impurities from his remains are believed to be fixed in place, giving its wielder a power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat.

48.content:
The Fourth Descender is the Traveler. Nahida told them so in Sumeru (3.2), using Fatui intelligence that did not list the Traveler's twin as a Descender. Since Irminsul holds nothing on the Traveler, they kept their memories of Rukkhadevata and of the Balladeer when everyone else's were rewritten.

The Narzissenkreuz sensed the Traveler as a new variable in the world-formula (4.2). Skirk contrasted herself with the Traveler: she is passing through, while they are changing Teyvat's fate (5.7). The Traveler told Lauma openly that they are a Descender (6.0). In Snezhnaya (7.0-7.1), Ronova said a Descender's soul cannot be taken into the Ley Lines, and that the Heavenly Principles' tolerance for the Traveler is not endless.

key: wills that can rival an entire world
beings who could transcend the gods
49.content: Some people have tried to make use of the Descender idea. In Fontaine, Rene de Petrichor of the Narzissenkreuz Ordo studied ancient sources, decided that a true Descender is a will that can rival a world, and tried to become one to save Fontaine from its prophecy. He failed twice. Khaenri'ah, according to *Perinheri*, hoped beings who could transcend the gods would come from beyond the world, and none came in the writer's lifetime. Canon has not confirmed that a native of Teyvat can become a Descender.

50.content:
Erosion (also: curse of time, the curse of Time): Erosion, which some call "the curse of time", is the slow wearing-away that time works on long-lived beings. It is best known for eating away memory, but canon also describes it wearing down the body, the will and the spirit or soul. Gods, elemental dragons, adepti and the cursed, deathless Khaenri'ahns all suffer it. It does not strike everyone equally. The more powerful the being, the more dangerous its erosion becomes. Azhdaha's slide into madness, and the fear of erosion that drove the Raiden Shogun Ei toward "eternity", are the classic examples.

The Chinese and Japanese terms literally mean "abrasion" or "wear". The idea is grinding down, not sudden corruption. No one in canon has found a way to stop it: Morax's attempt to halt Azhdaha's erosion failed, and Ei could only try to wall herself off from it.

Established: - Erosion affects memory first and most visibly: beings forget faces, promises and even their own past decisions.
- It also wears down the body, the will and the spirit, and can turn a gentle being savage.
- It is tied to the passage of time; characters treat it as part of the natural order that cannot be stopped.

- Kun Jun (Azhdaha's benevolent consciousness) calls erosion "the world's greatest destroyer of memories" and says only memories rooted in powerful emotion survive for long, and even those fade (Zhongli's Story Quest, 1.5).
- Zhongli: "The greater the power, the greater the danger erosion may bring about." He calls sealing away his old friend Azhdaha one form of erosion he has endured himself, and he wonders whether giving up what one loves in order to keep to the right path is the erosion the Heavenly Principles impose on him. The Traveler suspects erosion played a part in his decision to step down as Geo Archon, and Zhongli does not deny it.
- The Raiden Shogun (the puppet) says that "as long as the Ley Lines flow, the relentless erosion of time will never stop" (2.5).
- Dainsleif: the curse of "immortality" denies death, yet body and soul keep being eroded until they are virtually nonexistent, "even if 'death' is not the form that this erosion takes" (2.6).

- Erosion is not the same as aging. Ei's puppet does not age, and Dainsleif's ring keeps resetting his body, but the mind can still erode. The Shogun was built to withstand the body's wear, while Ei hid her consciousness away to protect it.
- Will can resist it for a long time. Dainsleif called the Black Serpent Knights' will, surviving 500 years of erosion, "a miracle born from hopelessness."
- Erosion can be invoked as an accusation. The Shogun tested whether Ei's changed outlook was real growth or "irreversible erosion" (Farewell to the Past, 2.5).

Kinds: Canon and the wiki's reading of it distinguish four overlapping kinds. Mental erosion is loss of memory and growing confusion; Azhdaha forgot Morax's face, Liyue Harbor and the reason he had accepted his seal. Physical erosion is decay of the body; Ei's puppet exists to withstand it. Erosion of the will weakens resolve until a being abandons what it once pursued; Ei claims her will cannot be eroded. Erosion of the spirit is the loss of one's sense of self, ending in savagery or madness; Yae Miko says the spirit is susceptible to it, which is why Ei placed her consciousness in her sword. A single being can suffer several kinds at once: Azhdaha's boss description says he has been disfigured by "the various kinds of erosion" during his long imprisonment.

Accounts: - Azhdaha, speaking through Kun Jun: Morax shared some of his power to slow the erosion, but it was futile, because "everything returns to dust" by the natural order.
- Zhongli: erosion is a burden of the long-lived and powerful; he hints it is imposed by the Heavenly Principles.
- Ei and the Shogun: erosion is the enemy of eternity; everything the Shogun does is "for the sake of resisting erosion."
- Yae Miko (voice-over "About Us: Erosion"): shutting yourself away from the world may only accelerate erosion, because nobody is left to reflect you back at yourself. Companions should "shine a light for each other." This directly questions Ei's method of isolation.

- Makoto, Ei's twin and the previous Electro Archon, understood erosion as well as Ei did but chose to focus on the present: knowing a scene is fleeting is a reason to enjoy it more. Ei, by contrast, felt "the agony of erosion" on the day the dying Makoto passed her the blade and she became the true Raiden Shogun. Both details come from the same Raiden Shogun character story (Character Story 4).
- Dainsleif and Haden (Khaenri'ahns): erosion is the price of the curse of immortality, which spares them death but not decay.

Azhdaha: Azhdaha is the clearest case of erosion. The ancient Earth Dragon (a vishap) was befriended by Morax, given sight and allowed to live above ground, and helped humanity. Erosion slowly ground away his memories of his friend and of protecting Liyue Harbor. When miners disturbed the Ley Lines of the Chasm, his pain drove him to attack the people he had protected, and Morax and the adepti sealed him. In a last moment of clarity he agreed to be sealed, but erosion later took that memory too, so he came to believe Morax had betrayed him.

Ei and eternity: Ei's pursuit of "eternity" was in large part a defence against erosion. Fearing that her spirit would erode, she created the Shogun, a puppet meant to withstand wear, to rule Inazuma in her place. She then withdrew into the Plane of Euthymia, her inner world, to meditate undisturbed with her consciousness housed in her sword. The Shogun's voice-over says her body exists "to withstand wear and tear, that the one within might achieve Eternity."
Her first puppet, later known as Kabukimono and eventually the Wanderer, was an experiment to see whether erosion could be escaped; she judged him too fragile when he shed tears. Ei made the Shogun's rules hard to change, even for herself, in case she herself became an enemy of eternity. In the Raiden Shogun's Story Quest (2.5) the Shogun turned this against her, suspecting that Ei's new openness was erosion. Ei won their duel inside Makoto's consciousness. The Shogun then accepted that her present will was "not the product of erosion", though it noted that "a will that cannot be eroded has no way to embrace the future", and agreed to become her kagemusha.

Khaenriahns: After the Cataclysm 500 years ago, Khaenri'ahns were cursed with deathless "immortality". Dainsleif names Ronova as the one who inflicted this Curse of Immortality on him (Black Feathers Scattered at Parting, 7.1). It does not protect them from erosion. Many became hilichurls or Abyss monsters, and the Black Serpent Knights became Shadowy Husks, though some, like Halfdan, held on to their captain's face and their duty for centuries. In A Space and Time Without You (5.7), Haden says that his memories, spirit, emotions and personality have long been eroded and fragmented. Dainsleif's body is kept unchanged by a ring left to him by his elder brother Vedrfolnir, which keeps resetting its condition, but Haden says Dainsleif's memories are still subject to erosion. Even so, Dainsleif remembers more than any other surviving Khaenri'ahn, which is why the Abyss Order wanted his memories for the Loom of Fate.

Curse of time: In The Realm of Rocks, Act II of the Lantern Rite story A Lanternlit Ode to the Silver Moon (6.3), Zizhi, the "Second Deadly Self" of the White Horse Adeptus Zibai, speaks of "the curse of time" and "the memories this body holds". Xiao guesses she means erosion. Madame Ping recalls that ancient mountain clans regarded the White Horse Adeptus as a "daughter of Time". She remarks that time does not treat everyone equally: the longer one dwells in the world, the more it takes. The story first ran as a limited-time event and can now be replayed as a Story Quest. In it, Zizhi says the one who governs Time (Istaroth) froze the moment of Zibai's death, and that this power has been both a blessing and a prison to her ever since.

Open questions: - Whether the Heavenly Principles impose erosion deliberately, or whether it is simply the natural order: Zhongli only wonders aloud.
- How erosion relates to Istaroth and to time itself (see uncertainties).

- Whether anything can truly halt it. Morax's power failed for Azhdaha; Ei's isolation was challenged by Yae Miko; Dainsleif's ring preserves only the body.
- Whether beings outside Teyvat's records are affected. The wiki suggests erosion may touch only those recorded in the Irminsul, but no character says so.

Connections: Related concepts: the Heavenly Principles, the Ley Lines and Irminsul, Istaroth and time, the curse of the Khaenri'ahns and immortality. Key figures: Azhdaha, Zhongli, Ei and the Shogun, Yae Miko, Dainsleif, Haden, Zibai/Zizhi.

Not to be confused with Abyssal corrosion or Gosoythoth's English title "Dragon of Manifest Erosion" (Natlan). Those concern the Abyss's contamination, not time's wear. Nor is it the same as Holy Soil, which is literally soil erosion around Watatsumi.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): erosion is slow and personal. Show it as a long-lived being losing the names of old friends, repeating grudges whose reasons are gone, or growing colder or harsher across centuries. It is not a visible magical effect. Mortal humans do not talk about "erosion" in these terms; it is a concern of gods, adepti, dragons and the cursed Khaenri'ahns, and most ordinary people would not know the word in this sense.

Long-lived characters handle it differently: Zhongli with weary acceptance, Ei once with fear and isolation and now with resolve, Dainsleif with grim endurance. Do not invent a cure, a precise timescale or a fixed age at which it begins; canon says it varies. Do not present the wiki's links to Istaroth or the Irminsul as established fact.

51.content: Azhdaha, the ancient Earth Dragon of the Chasm, was Morax's friend and a protector of humans until erosion wore away his memories and reason. Morax shared his own power to slow it, without success. After miners damaged the Chasm's Ley Lines and Azhdaha ran amok, Morax and the adepti sealed him. In a last lucid moment he consented to the seal, but erosion stole that memory too, and he came to see the seal as betrayal. His benevolent consciousness, appearing as Kun Jun, told the story in Zhongli's Story Quest (1.5).

52.comment: Erosion: Ei, the Shogun and erosion
52.content: Ei feared that her spirit would erode. She built the Shogun puppet to rule in her stead and to withstand bodily wear, and she meditated in the Plane of Euthymia with her consciousness in her sword. In 2.5 the Shogun suspected that Ei's change of heart was erosion. Ei proved in a duel that it was not, and the Shogun became her kagemusha. Yae Miko warns Ei that isolating herself may only speed erosion up.

53.content: The Khaenri'ahns' curse of immortality denies them death but not erosion: body and soul wear away until they are "virtually nonexistent" (Dainsleif, 2.6). Haden admits his memories, spirit, emotions and personality are eroded and fragmented (5.7). Dainsleif's brother's ring resets his body, but his memories still erode, though he remembers more than any other surviving Khaenri'ahn.

54.content: In the 6.3 Lantern Rite story (The Realm of Rocks), Zizhi speaks of "the curse of time" and "the memories this body holds". Xiao suspects erosion, and Madame Ping remarks that time takes more from those who dwell longer in the world. Zizhi says the one who governs Time froze the moment of Zibai's death, binding Zizhi in a prison that is also a blessing.

55.content:
Eternal Moon (also: Aria's moon, moon of Aria): The Eternal Moon was the first and largest of the Three Moons, raised by the Dragon King Nibelung and governed by the goddess Aria, eldest of the Three Moon Sisters. Legend says its immense gravity, or Aria's immense kuuvahki, raised the ocean tides. In the war of funerary flame the Heavenly Principles shattered it; Aria, unable to live without her moon, died. Pieces fell to Teyvat like stardust, the rest was hidden behind the false sky, and a part of Aria's power condensed into the Eternal Moon Marrow. Unlike the Frost Moon, it has not returned.

Established: - Largest and first of the Three Moons; its goddess was Aria.
- Said to have caused the tides.
- Destroyed by the Heavenly Principles; Aria did not survive.

- Nibelung made the moons with Secret Source technology and raised them from the planet's crust at what is now Nod-Krai. In the Natlan Archon Quest (5.3), Mavuika described the fragment that appeared in the sky as an "Ancient Moon's Remnant", a relic of Secret Source technology from the age of the Ancient Dragons; the wiki reads this as the Eternal Moon.
- Its goddess shared sovereignty of the night sky with her sisters, one at a time, riding in a silver carriage. The English text says they switched about three times a month; the Chinese uses the unit xun, which is looser.
- Part of Aria's power condensed into the Eternal Moon Marrow after her death. The Frostmoon Scions found it and kept it as a sacred relic.

- When it fell, heaven and earth were thrown into chaos, according to an artifact text (Moonlit Offering's Silver Crown). Some of its remains rained down onto Teyvat.
- Aria is shown as a tall, fair woman with long blonde hair in white and turquoise robes, with a soft yellow crescent behind her to mark her moon.

History: Nibelung raised the moon and left. When the Heavenly Principles arrived, Aria welcomed them as a guest and waited to see whether they would help the world. After Nibelung returned and imprisoned the sisters, the Heavenly Principles shattered the moon.

Before the war, Xiuhcoatl visited the moons looking for Nibelung and got only silence from each; canon does not say whether the sisters chose it. After the Heavenly Principles overthrew the Seven Sovereigns, Aria and her sisters entered a precarious peace with them, which the dragons took as betrayal. Aria, like her sisters, was appalled by the Heavenly Principles' treatment of civilisations that challenged the new rules.

When Nibelung returned from the Abyss, the sisters disagreed about taking sides. He read it as disloyalty, sealed them in the moon's reflection and made their moons into weapons. The Heavenly Principles shattered the Eternal and Iridescent Moons and threw the Frost Moon beyond the false sky. The dragons celebrated.

Aria survived inside the moon's reflection even after her moon was destroyed, because of the prison's warped properties, and knew nothing of the outside war. In True Moon (6.3) a future Columbina reached her and her sisters and told them what had happened. Aria accepted her death calmly and tried to comfort Sonnet. The three gave Columbina the authority of all three moons, and at their request she sent their now-mortal bodies back to Teyvat, where, as history records, they died. Aria's remains then formed the Marrow.

The marrow: The Eternal Moon Marrow was kept by the Frostmoon Scions as a relic. In Song of the Welkin Moon it was stolen from them and then lodged in the Traveler's body for safekeeping, until Dottore took it after Moon-Prayer Night (6.2). Columbina retrieved it in the final battle (6.3) and returned it to the Scions under the Moonchanter Lauma.

Dottore combined the Eternal and Iridescent Marrows with an artificial marrow he built, briefly becoming a false moon god. Authority drawn from marrows proved weaker than the sisters' own gift to Columbina, and the artificial marrow was destroyed when he was beaten.

Present day: In the Natlan Archon Quest (5.1), Mavuika's strike broke the false sky for a moment and revealed the Eternal Moon's shattered remnants; the sky closed again and the public was told it was an astronomical anomaly. Later the Fatui pulled fragments of the Eternal Moon down into Nod-Krai and built the Kuuvahki Experimental Design Bureau around one of them, for a project for the Tsaritsa that canon leaves unspecified. As of 7.1 the moon itself remains shattered, though its Marrow is held by Lauma.

The shadowmoon, an illusion the Heavenly Principles hung in the false sky to hide the moons' fates, faded once the Frost Moon returned to Teyvat's sky (6.3). The Eternal Moon had no such return.

Accounts: - Liyue books give a legend of three sister goddesses in a Lunar Palace; some versions say the sisters killed one another or that only two died. Treat these as folk memory.
- Dragon-side accounts treat the sisters as traitors to Nibelung.
- The sisters' own account (given to Columbina) is that they chose to wait and see the new order.

- Mavuika treats the moon fragment as a made object, a relic of Secret Source technology; the sisters and the Three Moons wiki account speak of living moons that are extensions of Nibelung's will.
- Where the moon's remnants lie is told two ways: pieces fell on Teyvat, while the rest was hidden beyond the false sky.

Open questions: - How Aria died is not told.
- Canon does not say what the Fatui weapon built around the moon fragment is.

- Whether "Aralos" on the teaser note is another name for Aria is unconfirmed.
- Whether the moon's draconic technology and its nature as Aria's seat are the same thing.

Connections: Aria (its goddess); Nibelung (creator); the Heavenly Principles (destroyers); the false sky and shadowmoon (what hid it); the Eternal Moon Marrow, kuuvahki and the Frostmoon Scions; Columbina, Lauma and Dottore (what became of its power); the Frost Moon and the Iridescent Moon (siblings).

56.content: The Eternal Moon Marrow condensed from Aria's power after her death. The Frostmoon Scions kept it as a relic; it was stolen, held in the Traveler's body for safekeeping, taken by Dottore, and returned by Columbina to the Scions under Lauma.

57.comment: Eternal Moon: Eternal Moon fragments in Nod-Krai
57.content: The Fatui dragged fragments of the shattered Eternal Moon down into Nod-Krai and built the Kuuvahki Experimental Design Bureau around one. The purpose is described only as an unspecified weapon for the Tsaritsa.

58.content:
False Sky (also: firmament, Teyvat's false sky, split-sky phenomenon, split-sky phenomena): The false sky, also called the firmament, is a real, physical barrier wrapped around the world of Teyvat. The Heavenly Principles made it to shut Teyvat off from the sea of stars and hide it from the wider universe. From inside it looks like an ordinary sky with an ordinary moon and stars; most people in Teyvat have no idea it is not real. The Heavenly Principles themselves are called "the great ruler of the firmament".

For centuries the false sky was a whispered theory. Scaramouche, the Doctor, King Deshret and Khaenri'ahn astrologers hinted at it. Since then it has been visibly broken several times by "split-sky phenomena": over Natlan in 5.1, and over Nod-Krai in 6.3, when the Frost Moon broke through and took the false moon's place in the night sky.

Established: - It surrounds the whole planet and separates Teyvat from the cosmos beyond, which canon calls the sea of stars.
- Its makers are the Heavenly Principles (also named Phanes), the First Descender, who rule Teyvat from Celestia.
- From inside, it projects the image of a normal sky. The stars and the single moon that Teyvat saw for millennia were part of that image.
- It can be breached. Only enormous power has done so on screen, and so far each breach has closed again.

- The book Before Sun and Moon (The Byakuyakoku Collection, vol. 2) describes Phanes using the shell of the egg it hatched from to split "the universe" from "the microcosm of the world." Lore readers take this eggshell to be the false sky.
- Canon calls the boundary "the world's borders". Alice, called the "Sustainer of the World's Borders" in Skirk's voice-overs, writes in the Wings of Feasting item text that Teyvat's borders "have grown fragile these past two years".
- After Dottore's defeat in 6.3, Nicole says that the crisis at the world's borders has made Teyvat easier to detect from the outside universe.

- The old moons were hidden behind it. After the War of Funerary Flame, the remains of the shattered Eternal Moon and the darkened Frost Moon lay beyond the false sky. The Heavenly Principles put an illusory "shadowmoon" onto the false sky to cover up what had happened to the Three Moons (wiki summary of the Three Moons and the 6.3 Archon Quest).
- Columbina reveals that the Traveler's spaceship had been hidden all along on the Frost Moon, "which lay beyond the sky" (Welkin Moon's Homecoming, 6.3).

Origin: The Moon Gazing world quests (6.7) tie the false sky to dragon research on the Frost Moon. The dragon researcher Lusalim led Project Lunar Veil, a plan to hide the moon behind a reflective veil made from Blackbody Matter. He feared that the message Project Moongazer was beaming into space might draw a hostile answer. A small Lunar Veil worked on Ungien's Circle. But before the full-sized veil generator could hide the whole moon, an entity from beyond the stars pierced it, and the laboratory exploded. The Traveler and Columbina suspect that entity was "the great ruler of the firmament", the Heavenly Principles.

Before proof: Scaramouche, visibly shaken by something he had just discovered in his research, told Mona and the Traveler that "the stars, the sky" are "a gigantic hoax". It happened during the 1.1 event Unreconciled Stars.

- Mona had been taught to speak of the "false sky" in her astrological readings. Scaramouche's outburst made her wonder whether the phrase was more than a figure of speech. Her teacher is Barbeloth.
- In Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies (3.2), the Doctor asked Nahida whether she had heard the rumour that "the skies of Teyvat are fake", and called it the secret about the world's "truth" hidden in Irminsul. He told her this as part of the deal that gave him the Dendro Gnosis.

- King Deshret's account in the Staff of the Scarlet Sands story says the angel Nabu Malikata described a night sky with three moons, and insists there should be three. He adds "even if the celestial sphere was just an illusion".
- Khaenri'ahn astrologers, branded heretics, saw in the Sign of Apaosha an "inverted image" of the false sky that revealed the origin of fate (Crimson Moon's Semblance). In Sumeru, the Sign of Apaosha shows the sea of stars beyond the false sky. The wiki records Barbeloth's view that it makes space unstable and easier to "break through the firmament".
- In The Splendorous Sky That Day (3.6), the Order of Skeptics' leader Nasejuna compares the sky to a reflection on water: an illusion that still hides the truth within it. This suggests the false sky mirrors something real.

Split sky phenomena: Visible breaches of the false sky are called split-sky phenomena. In 5.1, Mavuika's final strike against the Abyss over Natlan broke through the sky. In 6.3 the Doctor tore it open over Nod-Krai, and the returning Frost Moon then smashed through it.

- Natlan (5.1, The Rainbow Destined to Burn): in No One Fights Alone, Mavuika gathered the strength of the six modern heroes and Ronova's power and struck down the Abyssal entity Gosoythoth. The blow pierced the sky and briefly showed space beyond, with the shattered remains of the Eternal Moon. The breach soon closed. Mavuika said she had heard the phrase "false sky" before, but this was the first proof she had seen. The Adventurers' Guild knew of no such phenomenon in any other nation. She told the public it was an "astronomical anomaly".
- Nod-Krai (6.3, True Moon): as the "Heretic of the False Moon", Dottore used the power of the Moon Marrows to draw a line across the false sky. It split open to show the Frost Moon, and he rained attacks down from it. Using that opening, Nicole channelled her power through Varka and the Knave to drag the Frost Moon in. Dottore sealed the rift, but the moon's momentum shattered the barrier anyway, and Columbina came down with it. This completed Sandrone's plan to bring her back.

- Faint fragments still show in Natlan's sky north of the Great Volcano. The NPC Mtwa confirms they can be seen only from inside Natlan. In When All Becomes a Monument (5.3), Mavuika identifies them as "Ancient Moon's Remnants", relics of Secret Source technology from the age of the ancient dragons, and links them to a project of the Doctor's.
- After 6.3 the Frost Moon remains inside the false sky and has replaced the false moon. Columbina declares that the Frost Moon "has now entered the false sky" and that she is the Trilune Goddess. Ordinary people noticed the moon looked different, but most carried on as usual.

Skirk crossing: The animated short Star Odyssey (June 2025, announced in the 5.7 special programme) shows the first known crossing. Surtalogi, one of Skirk's mentors, opened the border so Skirk could descend into Teyvat, and Skirk is shown looking at the hole in the false sky. People in Teyvat saw her descend; whether anyone saw the rift itself is unknown.

Shadowmoon: The false moon on the false sky, called the shadowmoon or moon's reflection, was the Heavenly Principles' cover story for the lost Three Moons. Istaroth used it to hold Ziju, one of the Three Deadly Selves keeping a part of Zibai's soul, after Zibai died stalling a Celestial Nail aimed at Lang-Gan. Once the Frost Moon was back inside the false sky, the shadowmoon went invisible except during eclipses. Zhongli expected the wishes made at Lantern Rite to speed up its collapse. In A Lanternlit Ode to the Silver Moon (6.3), he and the Traveler reunited Zibai's three selves on Lantern Rite night. The shadowmoon fell apart moments later.

Accounts: - As a gift or a shelter: Before Sun and Moon presents the eggshell separation as part of Phanes's creation of the world and of humanity.
- As a cage: in the Springs of Hidden Jade item text, Zibai feels "trapped within the shell of the starry sky". In his friendship dialogue, Neuvillette, the Hydro Dragon Sovereign, says a world you cannot break out of is "a prison" and tells the Traveler not to fear the desolation outside it.
- As a lie: Scaramouche calls the sky a hoax. The Doctor treats it as Irminsul's hidden truth.

Open questions: - Is the false sky built directly on Lusalim's Lunar Veil? Strongly suggested, not stated.
- How large is it, and how far out? The Star Odyssey short shows it hugging the planet, yet the Frost Moon now orbits inside it, apparently much farther out.
- What exactly do Alice's "world's borders" mean, and how does her role relate to the Heavenly Principles?

Connections: The Heavenly Principles and Celestia made it and rule beneath it. The sea of stars lies beyond it, along with the Descenders who came through it: the Traveler, Skirk and others. Inside it sit the Three Moons story, the shadowmoon, the Frost Moon's return and Columbina, and the Natlan war against the Abyss.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): for almost everyone in Teyvat the sky is simply the sky. Scholars, Fatui researchers and the gods involved know better, and Natlanese and Nod-Krai witnesses saw something strange. Ordinary Natlanese accept the "astronomical anomaly" story. Do not have common folk talk about the false sky as a known fact.

Since 6.3 the moon over Teyvat is the real Frost Moon, not the old image. A character who looks up after that point sees a moon that has changed. Avoid scenes where mortals casually travel through or past the false sky. Canon breaches needed an Archon's full strength, Moon Marrow power or a Descender's mentor.

59.content: A split-sky phenomenon is a visible break in the false sky. One opened over Natlan in 5.1, when Mavuika's strike against Gosoythoth showed the Eternal Moon's fragments, which can still be faintly seen from Natlan. Another opened over Nod-Krai in 6.3, when Dottore tore the sky and the Frost Moon broke through. Both closed afterwards. Mavuika publicly called the first one an "astronomical anomaly".

60.comment: False Sky: Project Lunar Veil and the false sky
60.content: Lusalim, a dragon researcher on the Frost Moon, designed a veil to hide the moon from anyone who might answer Project Moongazer's broadcast. An entity from beyond the stars, which Columbina suspects was the Heavenly Principles, pierced his full-scale veil generator and destroyed the laboratory. Lusalim later surrendered his research to them, which he recorded as a sin against dragonkind. Columbina notes how closely the veil resembles the false sky; that it was the false sky's basis is inferred, not stated.

61.comment: False Sky: Great ruler of the firmament
61.content: "The great ruler of the firmament" is an epithet for the Heavenly Principles. Columbina uses it in the Nod-Krai story (Welkin Moon's Homecoming, 6.3) and again in the Moon Gazing world quests (6.7), and Danica uses it in the 7.0 Snezhnaya Archon Quest. It names them as the power behind the false sky.

62.content:
Fate (also: Heimarmene, Fortuna, wheel of fate, Musica Mundana, Sourcesong, threads of fate, fate of Teyvat, predetermined fate): Fate is the predetermined destiny of Teyvat, imposed by the Heavenly Principles through Irminsul and the stars. Canon also calls it Heimarmene, and in Fontaine and Remuria it was called Fortuna. Vision bearers are tied to named constellations. Descenders are not bound in the same way.

Fate is not a god who acts. It is closer to a written script that the world was refashioned to follow. Characters speak of it as something to accept, hide from or break. Hyperborea's Saint rose against it, Remuria and Sumeru built systems meant to stand apart from it, and Durin is the one fate shown on screen being rewritten on purpose.

Established: - The Heavenly Principles repurposed Irminsul into the world's anchor of fate. Apep says they usurped and remade the tree and used it to anchor the fate of the world (Song of the Welkin Moon Act IX, 6.6).
- Stars record fate: a Vision bearer's fate is tied to a constellation made of Stella Fortuna.

- Nahida says the prophecy of Fontaine was carved into Irminsul long ago, and that Focalors was smart enough to turn the fate of the world around anyway (voice-over about Furina).
- Barbeloth tells the Traveler that a Descender's fate is not anchored in Teyvat. Mona cannot read the Traveler or Paimon in the stars either.

- Names: Fate, Heimarmene (the Belyi Tsar's notes, the Narzissenkreuz Ordo) and Fortuna (Fontaine, Remuria). Item text also gives wheel of fate, Musica Mundana and Sourcesong.
- In the Chamber of Deliberation records, one of the Thirteen Sovereign Lords (CL-03) abstains from a vote, saying the fate of "these soulless creatures bound to star signs" does not concern them.
- Mona, who reads the reflection of the stars in water, says fate cannot be changed or reversed, only accepted. Astrologers avoid reading their own fate because it can turn fate in on itself, and advising a subject risks tangling the reader's fate with theirs.
- The Narzissenkreuz Ordo taught that to receive a Vision is to sell oneself to the world's bound fate, Heimarmene (their Note #2 in Fontaine).
- Citlali, a Natlan shaman, says the heavens control human fate like a puppeteer and a marionette, so the inauspicious stars have no free will. She seals the power of inauspicious stars into dolls bound with animal bones, and in a birthday letter says her Tzitzimitl Citlalin was made by binding her own Stella Fortuna.
- The Little Witch and the Undying Fire calls the stars of Teyvat the heavenly strings that bind humans, and says other cosmic forces are weakened by a giant sky-shroud, which is the false sky.
- In The Solution of Fate (6.2) Albedo, recalling what Barbeloth told them, says the fate of every living being in Teyvat is woven into the fabric of time, so its most natural path is to proceed along its given track.
- In 7.0, notes at the Pale Crown Palace record that Hyperborea's destruction had been decreed long before Anacharsis, and that the Belyi Tsar feared his conclusion about Heimarmene too terrible to write down.

Names: - Heimarmene: the name used in the Belyi Tsar's notes and by the Narzissenkreuz Ordo. It comes from a Greek word meaning what has been allotted.
- Fortuna: the Fontainian and Remurian word, linked to the harp-string image. It is also the name of an imperial ship in The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria.
- In the Lightless Silk String item text, ancient Fontainians thought Fortuna ruled the world and was woven from countless fibres like harp strings. Music in harmony would bring happiness to all, and discord would tear the fabric of the universe.
- Remus's Grand Symphony, which Phobos was meant to carry out, is sometimes called Fortuna, and Remus is called the king of Fortuna in one weapon text.

Pale crown notes: The notes at the Pale Crown Palace are the Belyi Tsar's private record of his expeditions into the Shadow Realm and the ruins of Hyperborea. They are the longest canon account of how Fate works, and they are also one person's conclusions.
- Note II: he judges that Hyperborea fell to a Celestial Nail sent from above, and he doubts that help from the angels would have changed the outcome.
- Note IV: the records beside the Eitr show that Hyperborea's fate was sealed before The Saint (Anacharsis) arrived. Even the eldest daughter of the angels (Koitar) could not alter the decree, and those who stayed faithful to the future could only stave off its execution for thirty years. He states that his conclusion about Heimarmene may be too terrible to write. He argues that when people anchor themselves to fate, the Abyss will anchor itself to them at the end of time.
- He also writes that the Goddess of Flowers in Sumeru and the woman who prophesied the rising waters in Fontaine each tried to build systems independent of both the Ley Lines and Heimarmene, and that even small rents can loosen the threads of fate. He cites the Natlan ruler who is not a divinely anointed Sacred Lord and the Remurians who evaded the gaze of the heavens.

Attempts to escape: Several civilisations tried to build something that would not answer to Fate. None of them ended well, but each left a mark, according to the Belyi Tsar.

- Hyperborea: The Saint (Anacharsis) launched an advance against the fate that ruled the world and was punished. Those faithful to the future delayed the decreed end by thirty years, but even Koitar could not alter it.
- Remuria: Remus and Sybilla made Phobos, the Grand Symphony, to avert the prophecy of Fontaine; the Tsar's Note IV says she who prophesied the rising waters sought a system independent of the Ley Lines and Heimarmene. Remurian souls were bound to Phobos and given golem bodies. It failed to save Remuria, but the Tsar writes that the Remurians still eluded the gaze of the high heavens and passed on their arts in distorted form. The wiki links those arts to the Golden Troupe, the Marechaussee Phantom and the Narzissenkreuz Ordo.
- Sumeru: King Deshret's Aaru was meant to be a new afterlife outside the gods' reach, built with celestial technology from the angel Nabu Malikata. The Tsar's Note IV says the Goddess of Flowers sought to build a system independent of the Ley Lines and Heimarmene.

Durin: In the Draco Rubedo Chapter the Hexenzirkel's Andersdotter sends a story-born Durin into Teyvat. Albedo explains that the book Durin's story had been grafted onto the fate of the historical Durin, so that one Durin's fate overwrote the other. In The Solution of Fate the Traveler's party faces a trial in the form of "Fate", which says it cannot die and has been decreed by fate. Durin refuses it. Barbeloth afterwards finds that this Durin's fate no longer appears among the stars. Anya says only he can defy the fate of this world. Irminsul at first rejected him; the Hexenzirkel and the Traveler arranged for the Ley Lines to accept him as a separate being.

Irminsul and aaru: In Song of the Welkin Moon Act X (6.6), Nahida and her allies burn the corrupted Irminsul with the Pyro Gnosis, to stop Dottore's experiment. The three Shades of the Heavenly Principles present, Ronova, Istaroth and Naberius, ask whether she is sure, and Nahida answers that humanity's survival matters more than the tree; they let her proceed. The reconfigured Aaru then takes over the role of storing and collecting information, with no lasting harm to Nahida or Nicole.

Accounts: - As a script: Mona speaks of fate as fixed and best accepted.
- As a lie: in 7.1 the Tsaritsa (Anastasya) says civilisation is a lie told to us by fate, and the Shades of the Heavenly Principles (Life, Death, Time, Space) are everywhere (Light and Shadow, Intertwined). The Traveler asks whether her authority is rebellion against fate.

- As something that can be bent: Durin, the Remurians and the Abyss Order treat it as something to loosen, rewrite or weave anew. The Abyss Order's device is called the Loom of Fate, built to weave Ley Lines.
- As a puppeteer's strings: Citlali and the Little Witch text use the image of strings that bind people from the heavens above.

Open questions: - Who or what actually writes each fate, and does any individual choice matter inside the pattern? Canon is not consistent.
- What did Aaru's takeover from Irminsul change for Fate?
- How does Fate relate to the Abyss? The Belyi Tsar's notes say that anchoring into fate draws the Abyss in, but he states this as his own conclusion.
- Why Descenders stand outside Fate, and what that implies for the Traveler.

Connections: The Heavenly Principles and Celestia imposed Fate; Irminsul and the false sky are its instruments. Descenders such as the Traveler stand outside it. Constellations and Stella Fortuna are its visible form, and Visions bind their bearers to it. Remuria, Hyperborea, Sumeru's Aaru, Natlan and Fontaine's prophecy are all stories of struggle with it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): most people in Teyvat do not think of "Fate" as a cosmic system. They say fate, destiny or luck as ordinary words. Only astrologers, scholars of Remuria and Khaenri'ah, Descenders and the very old know that Heimarmene is real and imposed. Do not have common folk lecture about the Heavenly Principles.

When a character talks about fate, check what they plausibly know. A Mondstadt knight may speak of destiny. A Hexenzirkel witch, Mona, Nahida, Nicole, the Fatui and the Abyss Order can speak of it as a system. Characters should not claim that Fate is broken or destroyed as of 7.1: Irminsul burned and Aaru replaced it, but the stars still stand.

63.content: Heimarmene is the name the Belyi Tsar and the Narzissenkreuz Ordo use for the predetermined fate of Teyvat. They treat it as imposed by the Heavenly Principles, and the Ordo warns that accepting a Vision binds one to it. The Tsar's notes in the Pale Crown Palace (7.0) say its truth was too terrible for him to write down.

64.content: Fortuna is the Fontainian word for fate. Ancient Fontainians pictured it as a harp with strings of countless fibres, where harmony brought joy and dissonance tore the world. Remuria, which built its culture around music, used the word for its Grand Symphony and for its prophesied fall, and Remus, the king of Fortuna, made Phobos to escape the prophecy. The sources are the Lightless Silk String item text and The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria.

65.comment: Fate: Stella Fortuna and star signs
65.content: Stella Fortuna are the stars that make up the constellations, and each Vision bearer's fate is linked to a constellation; astrologers hold that the stars map out a Vision bearer's past, present and future. Citlali says she made her Tzitzimitl Citlalin by binding her own Stella Fortuna. The wiki notes that special constellations depicting the person are shown for the Traveler, the Archons, the adepti and a few others.

66.content: During the limited-time event Unreconciled Stars (1.1), meteorites fell on Mondstadt that had once been part of a constellation: that of Leonard, an adventurer of some two thousand years ago who dreamed of climbing Pilos Peak. His will carried in the fallen stars sent people who touched them into a deep sleep in which they dreamt of the climb. Canon does not explain why the constellation fell.

67.content: Mona and her teacher Barbeloth read fate in the inverted reflection of the stars on water, which they call hydromancy. Mona says the best water is melted snow, that she will not read her own fate, and that advice tangles a reader's fate with the subject's. She cannot read the Traveler or Paimon.

68.content: Barbeloth tells the Traveler that a Descender's fate is not anchored in Teyvat (Revelations by Chance, 6.7). Mona says she cannot give the Traveler a prediction because they are not from this world, and cannot discern anything of Paimon's fate. No source fully explains why Descenders stand outside the pattern.

69.comment: Fate: Fate and the Natlan war
69.content: After Xiuhcoatl bowed its head, Ronova appeared before Xbalanque and showed him the arc of fate: all life devoured by boundless darkness in the eternal Abyss, so Natlan knew a new war had begun (A Thousand Blazing Suns). During the final fight in 5.3, a Voice in the Void tells Mavuika her destruction is inevitable and that the lives of Descenders are more valuable than she can imagine; she answers, "If I was fated to fail, then why do you fear?"

70.content: In The Solution of Fate (6.2) the story Durin of Andersdotter's book defeats a trial called "Fate" and afterwards no longer has a fate among the stars, according to Barbeloth. It is the only fate shown to have been rewritten on purpose.

key: Notes by a Certain Noble Individual
71.comment: Fate: Notes at the Pale Crown Palace
71.content: The six notes of the Belyi Tsar in his mausoleum record his forays into the Shadow Realm and Hyperborea. They give the fullest canon account of Heimarmene, its link to the Abyss, and the systems that tried to stand apart from it. They are one man's reconstruction from records and are partly censored.

72.content: The Abyss Order uses "Loom of Fate" for an operation and a device. Chlothar first used the phrase for his son Caribert, and later it came to mean a machine that can weave Ley Lines into the planet. The Traveler's sibling is using it, and has used it to weave the Ley Lines of New Khaenri'ah. The name is a metaphor; it does not mean the Abyss Order has taken control of Fate.

73.comment: Fate: The golden harp of fate
73.content: Two texts from the limited-time event Clink Clank Clash (6.0) picture fate as music. The Etherlight Spindlelute's story says the titan craftsman of the skies once wove the destinies of all living beings, with a golden harp as the instrument of fate. The Golden Strings material says some in a long-lost civilisation believed the fate governing the world was a song from a colossal harp hung in the heavens, because they had seen angels pluck golden strings from the skies. Both are poetic in-universe accounts, not a description of the mechanism.

74.content:
Four Shades (also: Four Great Rulers, Shades of the Heavenly Principles, Shadows of the Heavenly Principles): The Four Shades, or Four Great Rulers, are four gods the Heavenly Principles created as "shades" of itself during its war against the Seven Sovereigns. Each governs one law of the world: Naberius (Life), Ronova (Death), Istaroth (Time) and Asmoday (Space). They are older and stronger than The Seven and act from Celestia as the Heavenly Principles' emissaries. As of 7.1, Naberius survives only fused with the alchemist Rhinedottir, Ronova has lost her Authority and died, Istaroth is active but elusive, and Asmoday has defected.

Few mortals know they exist. They dislike being named by any living being, prefer to stay in the shadows, and usually act through proxies, curses and lent power rather than open rule.

Established: - Origin: Enkanomiya's chronicle Before Sun and Moon says that when the Primordial One fought the dragon-lords of the old world, it created shining shades of itself, "and the number of these shades was four". Forty years later the Sovereigns were vanquished.
- Role and rank: they govern Teyvat's fundamental laws for the Heavenly Principles. Mavuika calls Ronova a god "whose existence predates any Archon", a kind of emissary of the Heavenly Principles. The Jester calls the Shades "beings of an altogether higher order".
- Command: they receive directives from Celestia and do not appear able to act wholly on their own initiative, so they look for ways to act "within the rules".

- Appearance: the Shades share a family likeness, each a tall woman with pale skin and long white hair; the three whose faces are shown have golden eyes whose pupils suit their domains (Istaroth's resemble a clock face without hands, Ronova's a seven-petalled flower, Asmoday's a target). Naberius's original face has never been clearly shown.
- Ronova dismisses the Tsaritsa's powers as "paltry"; Istaroth is called a "higher power" than Makoto. Paimon describes the Shades as having "the power to enforce the rules of the world itself".
- Lent and stolen power: a Shade can grant part of her Authority to others, and it can also be stolen or usurped without her consent (sub-entry "Borrowed and stolen Authority").
- Joint power: Ronova says that if Asmoday returned, the Four Shades could "jointly activate" their Authority.

Members: Naberius, Ruler of Life (now inside Rhinedottir); Ronova, Ruler of Death and Arbiter of the Heavenly Principles (dead as of 7.1); Istaroth, Ruler of Time; Asmoday, Ruler of Space and Sustainer of the Heavenly Principles (defected).

Each has her own entry. Naberius, whose compassion was revered from Hyperborea to Sal Vindagnyr, had her heart devoured by Rhinedottir after the Cataclysm; she lost her agency but still objects from within their shared mind. Ronova could define or deny any death, as when she cursed full-blooded Khaenri'ahns with immortality. Istaroth is bored and quietly bends history. Asmoday stopped the twin travelers leaving Teyvat 500 years ago and is now seen with the Traveler's sibling.

Other names: Naberius is Mother of Life and, to the Frostmoon Scions, Maadteraahka. Ronova is Mother of the Underworld, Grim Reaper and, to the Frostmoon Scions, Tuonetar. Istaroth was Kairos and Tokoyo Ookami in Enkanomiya and is said to remember everything while letting everything be forgotten. Asmoday kept a private domain, the Temple of Space.

Present day: As of 7.1 the Heavenly Principles is still dormant. The Shades meet in Celestia, but Asmoday has missed every meeting since the Cataclysm. In Snezhnaya, Ronova broke the rules with a curse of death; Celestia reclaimed her Authority, Pierro mortally wounded her, and she died.

- Natlan (Natlan Archon Quest): Mavuika spent the power Xbalanque had borrowed from Ronova to defeat the Abyss. Ronova came to take Mavuika's life as payment, but Capitano offered his own, and Ronova chose to keep her curse of immortality on him.
- Sumeru (Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, 6.6): when Nahida invoked her right as Irminsul's keeper to burn the corrupted tree with the Pyro Gnosis, Ronova, Istaroth and Naberius appeared, questioned her and allowed it. Naberius said Nahida had herself become "a great tree".
- Snezhnaya (7.0-7.1): Ronova cursed people working toward technology that threatened the Heavenly Principles, starting with Project Mistilteinn's researchers. Dying, she placed the Eitr on the Celestial Nail above the Cryo Dragon's corpse; the nail began to crumble as she disintegrated, calling it her "parting gift", and the other Celestial Nails across Teyvat reacted.

Rules and monitoring: The Shades are watched by a "monitoring cycle" the Heavenly Principles set up to catch violations; breaking the rules can cost a Shade her Authority.

Ronova's curse of death killed people and needed Rhinedottir's Authority of Life to revive them before a cycle ended. When the Tsaritsa delayed the revival, Celestia detected it and reclaimed Ronova's Authority of Death. A directive then "echoed" in Rhinedottir's mind ordering her to put Ronova's mistake right. Rhinedottir noted Celestia was watching her and Naberius closely and that she did not want to lose the Authority of Life too. Even without her Authority, Ronova kept power befitting a Shade until Pierro wounded her.

Authorities: In Delusion (Chapter VII) (7.1), The Knave explains that the Authorities of Life, Death, Time and Space once belonged to the Three Moons, the Iridescent Moon holding the largest share of Death. After the moons' destruction in the War of Funerary Flame, the Heavenly Principles reclaimed them and redistributed them among the Four Shades "under a new system of rules". The Unified Civilization had already worshipped the Shades as masters of these domains.

History: In the ancient world the Shades were worshipped openly. Arcadia built the Thousand Winds Temple for Istaroth and the Temple of Space for Asmoday. After the War of Funerary Flame most of humanity forgot them.
- Natlan: Ronova guided the Lord of the Night in creating the Night Kingdom to mend Natlan's ley lines. Later Xbalanque, the first Pyro Archon, borrowed her power to create Natlan's rules; they agreed she would deny involvement if the Heavenly Principles found out.
- Mondstadt: about 2,600 years ago Istaroth met the wind spirit who became Barbatos and entrusted him with fragments of her power.
- The Cataclysm: Ronova cursed the full-blooded Khaenri'ahns with immortality without separating guilty from innocent. Asmoday blocked and sealed the twin travelers.

The gods limits: The official teaser "The Gods' Limits" (2025-07-09) was the first time all four Shades were shown. Ronova, Istaroth and Rhinedottir (attending for Naberius) meet in Celestia. Ronova says no Shade has missed a meeting since the Heavenly Principles made them, until Asmoday. Istaroth calls the meetings a formality and suggests Asmoday "switched sides"; Ronova finds that unthinkable unless Asmoday loves a new master more than herself.

Accounts: - Lord of the Night: the Shades do not like being named by any living being, even The Seven, and prefer to remain in the shadows as Shades. He calls the one he knows only "the Ruler of Death".
- Ronova to her peers: "We are Shades, Shadows of the Heavenly Principles."
- Istaroth explains her interventions as a way to pass the time.

Open questions: Canon leaves open who now holds the Authority of Death, what Asmoday intends with the Traveler's sibling, and whether Istaroth truly serves the Heavenly Principles.

Also unexplained: how Naberius's heart ended up in a domain after the Cataclysm, and how the Shades will act when the Heavenly Principles wakes.

Connections: Heavenly Principles (creator and master); Celestia (their seat and source of directives); The Seven (younger gods who sometimes borrow their power); the Three Moons (former holders of the four Authorities); the Abyss and the Crimson Moon (a rival form of Death); Paimon (Ronova tried to seize her as a creation of Celestia).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the Shades as remote, rule-bound powers. Ordinary people do not know their names; Archons, Fatui leaders and Hexenzirkel mages might. A Shade appearing is a world-altering event. As of 7.1, do not portray Ronova alive, Naberius independent of Rhinedottir, or Asmoday back in Celestia.

Keep them distinct: Istaroth is idle, playful and evasive; Ronova was severe, contemptuous of mortals and bound by her own rules; Naberius is a disapproving inner voice; Asmoday is cold and absent.

75.comment: Four Shades: Rulers of Life, Death, Time and Space
75.content: The four titles of the Shades. Ruler of Life: Naberius, whose power and duties passed to Rhinedottir when Rhinedottir devoured her heart. Ruler of Death: Ronova, whose Authority Celestia reclaimed in 7.1 before she died. Ruler of Time: Istaroth. Ruler of Space: Asmoday, who has abandoned her post. The Knave says these four Authorities once belonged to the Three Moons.

76.content: A system the Heavenly Principles set up to check that the Shades obey the rules. Ronova and Rhinedottir agreed on a "window of resurrection" so that Ronova's victims would be revived before a cycle concluded. The Tsaritsa used her Cryo mastery and six Gnoses to slow time around Rhinedottir in Zapolyarny Palace, so the window passed, Celestia detected the aberration and reclaimed Ronova's Authority of Death.

77.comment: Four Shades: Borrowed and stolen Authority
77.content: Shades can lend fragments of their Authority, and it can be stolen. Istaroth entrusted fragments of her power to Barbatos. The Nameless Bard usurped Istaroth's power to save Mondstadt and died of it. Xbalanque borrowed Ronova's power to create Natlan's rules, at the price that its users would die. Koitar stole part of Naberius's Authority of Life for Hyperborea's artisans to make the Snowland Fae; it passed down to the Vila and to Vesna, until Rhinedottir took it back in 7.1.

78.comment: Four Shades: Asmoday's absence from Celestia
78.content: Since the Cataclysm Asmoday has missed every Shade meeting in Celestia, and her Temple of Space has been left to its keepers. Istaroth guessed she had switched sides; Ronova wanted her found. The Tsaritsa later saw her in Snezhnaya with a hooded figure, and Asmoday opened portals to escape. Her portals were also seen closing near the Traveler's meeting with their sibling in Natlan.

79.content:
Gnosis (also: Gnoses, Heart of God, Shen zhi Xin, Archon's Gnosis): A Gnosis (plural Gnoses) is a gleaming object shaped like a chess piece that an Archon of The Seven carries inside their chest. There are seven, one per element. Venti calls it an Archon's internal focus that resonates directly with Celestia and marks them as one of The Seven. Gnoses amplify elemental power and symbolise the Heavenly Principles' control over Teyvat. Since the Prologue the Tsaritsa's Fatui have been collecting them; as of 7.1 she holds six, and only the Pyro Gnosis is missing.

In Chinese and Japanese the name means "Heart of God", paired with Visions as the "Eye of God". Their origin was kept secret for millennia: they were made from the body of the Third Descender, Saarelainen (revealed in stages in 4.2 and 7.1).

Established: - An Archon does not need a Gnosis to use their element or keep their divine throne. Ei gave hers away centuries ago and is still the Electro Archon.
- A Gnosis can be torn out by force (Signora from Venti) or handed over willingly (Zhongli, Yae Miko, Neuvillette, Mavuika).

- Venti calls Visions "primitive tools" next to a Gnosis, which he describes as "a higher-order nexus of elemental manipulation". Mavuika calls it "basically an Elemental energy enhancer" that she rarely used. Nahida saw it as a core that gathers elemental power at her will.
- A Gnosis resists tampering: Ei tried and failed to modify hers into an energy supply device.
- Someone other than its own Archon normally struggles to use a Gnosis. Dottore told Nahida she could not fight with the Electro Gnosis. Still, Nahida used it to reach Greater Lord Rukkhadevata's consciousness, and the Wanderer could wield lightning only through heavy modifications made with Dottore and the Akademiya.
- A Gnosis can hold its bearer's obsessions. When Nahida pulled the Electro Gnosis out of Shouki no Kami, the Balladeer fell from the machine in despair.

- Archons may keep some sense of their Gnosis after giving it away: Mavuika "sensed its loss" when the Pyro Gnosis vanished.
- Beings partly outside the Heavenly Principles' laws, such as Neuvillette and the Traveler, have handled Gnoses without obvious trouble. The Traveler carried the Pyro Gnosis through Sumeru's barrier when it sank into their body "just like phlogiston".
- Nahida warned Dottore that destroying a Gnosis might wake the Heavenly Principles. Canon has not shown what would happen.

Origin: Origin, as canon now tells it. Neuvillette's character story (4.1) says the "usurper", the Heavenly Principles, was badly wounded in the war against Nibelung and could no longer suppress the world's original order by its own authority. With "one who came after" it created the seven Gnoses to keep that order, and the gods were driven to fight over them. In Finale (4.2), Skirk tells Neuvillette the Gnoses are remains of the Third Descender and calls them objects of misfortune, warning that once a person dies their bonds to the world turn into curses.

Black Feathers Scattered at Parting (7.1) gives the full account, told by Rhinedottir to the Tsaritsa from Celestia's records. Incited by the Belyi Tsar, Anastasya and the Third Descender, Saarelainen, opened a gate to the Abyss. The Heavenly Principles erased Anastasya from existence. Saarelainen went up to Celestia and offered his own life: he had an unmatched affinity for the Human Realm's power and could amplify the elements. He agreed to let his remains be split into seven pieces to consolidate the Heavenly Principles' rule. In return they would bring Anastasya back and never harm his descendants, the Khaenri'ahns. He bound the promise with a curse that would only work if it were broken. The Heavenly Principles also required that he be forgotten, and erased him from Irminsul.

Holders: As of 7.1: the Cryo Gnosis is the Tsaritsa's own. Signora took the Anemo and Geo Gnoses; Dottore got the Electro and Dendro; Arlecchino brought the Hydro. The Pyro Gnosis burned with Irminsul in 6.6 and has vanished.

- Anemo: Signora tore it from Venti's chest outside the Cathedral in Mondstadt (Prologue, 1.0).
- Geo: Zhongli handed it to Signora after his Rite of Parting, fulfilling a secret contract with the Tsaritsa, his "Contract to End All Contracts" (1.1). What she gave him in return is unrevealed.
- Electro: Ei left it with Yae Miko before retreating into the Plane of Euthymia. In 2.1 Miko traded it to Scaramouche (the Balladeer) for the Traveler's safety. Scaramouche built it into Shouki no Kami. Nahida took it from him in 3.2, then gave it to Dottore in exchange for his erasing his other segments.
- Dendro: Nahida gave her own Gnosis to Dottore in exchange for information about the false sky (3.2).
- Hydro: Focalors passed it to Neuvillette as her divinity faded. Neuvillette, now wary of it after Skirk's warning, gave it to Arlecchino as a "diplomatic gift" (4.2).
- Pyro: Capitano dueled Mavuika for it but then asked to be relieved of that mission, and the Tsaritsa agreed (5.3). In 6.6 Mavuika gave it to the Traveler for Nahida, who used it to burn the corrupted Irminsul.

Uses: Archons have used their Gnoses as power sources for national infrastructure.
- Liyue: the Golden House minted the world's Mora with the Geo Archon's power and has been shut since Zhongli gave up the Geo Gnosis.
- Sumeru: the Dendro Gnosis powered the Akasha, which Nahida shut down after taking back control (3.2).
- Fontaine: the Hydro Gnosis powered the Oratrice Mecanique d'Analyse Cardinale. Focalors used its stored energy to execute herself and destroy the Hydro throne (4.2).

Accounts: Most mortals know little or nothing about Gnoses. Venti said his was not something he was meant to discuss with ordinary people, and rank-and-file Fatui seem unaware of the Harbingers' mission.

Paimon describes Gnoses as what keeps The Seven connected to Celestia. Yae Miko said Ei had severed her ties with Celestia by giving hers up. Even so, canon treats Ei as the Electro Archon, Focalors's destruction of the Hydro throne left the Hydro Gnosis unharmed, and Nahida was never called anything but the Dendro Archon while holding other Gnoses. Zhongli told Azhdaha he was no longer the Geo Archon after losing his Gnosis, and Azhdaha said he could sense it. Canon leaves open how far Gnosis, throne and title depend on each other.

Open questions: - Where is the Pyro Gnosis? The Tsaritsa expects the Ley Lines to cast it out eventually.
- What is sealed beneath Zapolyarny Palace, and will it open with all seven Gnoses?
- What did the Tsaritsa give Zhongli for the Geo Gnosis?

- How exactly do the Gnoses maintain the Heavenly Principles' order, and what would happen if one were destroyed or all seven were gathered?
- Is Saarelainen's remaining power or will still present in the Gnoses? Canon hints at a link between them and Stellar Linchpins but explains nothing more.

Connections: The Seven and their divine thrones (Archon Authority is separate from the Gnosis); Visions (Neuvillette's story places their appearance in the same era, and Venti calls them primitive by comparison); the Tsaritsa's plan and the Fatui Harbingers; the Third Descender and the Khaenri'ahn bloodline; the dormancy of the Heavenly Principles.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat Gnoses as state secrets. Ordinary people, soldiers and most Fatui agents should not know what one is, let alone where they are. Archons speak of them guardedly. Mavuika and Zhongli were relaxed about parting with theirs, while the Wanderer was desperate to have one.

In scenes set after 7.1, the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses in Zapolyarny Palace, no Archon carries their own except her, and nobody knows where the Pyro Gnosis is. Do not return Gnoses to Venti, Zhongli, Nahida or anyone else, and do not show an Archon losing their element without one.

80.content: In the official teaser "A Winter Night's Lazzo", made for Signora's funeral in the Sanctuary of Grief, Pierro plays chess against an unseen opponent whose pieces move by themselves, implied to be the Tsaritsa. The Anemo and Geo Gnoses stand on the board as pieces. Later Snezhnaya trailers such as "Sudden Snow" use more Gnoses the same way. Which piece each represents is fan analysis, not canon. In Sumeru Dottore called the Gnosis "another chess piece".

81.content: In 6.6 Mavuika gave the Pyro Gnosis to the Traveler. At the edge of Sumeru's barrier it sank into their body, and Nahida drew it out during the battle against Dottore. It burst into flame that consumed the corrupted Irminsul. Afterwards Nahida and Mavuika found no trace of it, not even ash, and Mavuika felt it had gone. In 7.1 the Traveler told the Tsaritsa it had burned and, per Mavuika, returned to the Ley Lines. The Tsaritsa doubted that remains of the Third Descender could coexist with the Ley Lines for long, and expects it to resurface. Its fate is open.

82.content: Rhinedottir's account (7.1): Saarelainen let the Heavenly Principles split his remains into the seven Gnoses. In exchange they revived the erased Anastasya and swore never to harm the Khaenri'ahns, a promise guarded by a curse. Every memory of him was then erased from Irminsul. Only the Belyi Tsar, who had fled into the Shadow Realm, remembered. Anastasya does not remember Saarelainen and says she chooses to live in the present.

83.content:
God (also: Gods of Teyvat, Demon God, Majin, ancient gods, evil gods): Gods are immortal, supernatural beings that once led and oversaw the Human Realm of Teyvat. They are tied to Celestia, though several resented it. Many gods roamed Teyvat before the Archon War. Seven divine seats then opened up in Celestia, and the gods fought over them until about 2,000 years ago. Most were killed or sealed. The seven victors became the Archons, one per element and nation. Gods who refused to live under The Seven fled to islands in the Dark Sea and became "evil gods." Dead gods leave power, curses and remains behind.

A god is not the same as a Vision holder or a dragon. Vision holders are mortal "allogenes" who might one day ascend. Elemental dragons hold power equal to a god's. The English game text uses "Archon" for The Seven only; older gods are "gods," though the Chinese original calls them "demon gods" (Mo-shen). The word is unisex: Ei and Nahida are called gods, not goddesses.

Established: - Gods govern the Human Realm and hold its power. That power is incompatible with the Light Realm's and the Void Realm's under normal conditions.
- Their essence is effectively immortal. A slain god's emotions and obsessions linger and their power flows into the land.
- Gods can choose any form. Morax has appeared as a young man, a woman and an old man, and Zhongli is his latest vessel. Venti's vessel is modelled on the bard he once knew.

- How a god dies shapes what is left. A god killed against their will releases power that corrupts the area, as Havria did when her own followers murdered her, or leaves lingering curses of death, disease and madness (the Tatarigami is the clearest case). A god who chooses to die can release power in a controlled way, as Boreas and Marchosius did. Remus's death caused no corruption; his will kept the ruins of Capitolium well preserved for 2,000 years.
- Remains can be sealed or neutralised. When Egeria died in the Cataclysm, Greater Lord Rukkhadevata made the Harvisptokhm from the Amrita her death left behind and used it against the Abyss; Raiden Shogun raised the Narukami Pillars on Yashiori Island to suppress Orobashi's curse. Remains injected into a human can cause madness, drastic personality change or unusual powers.
- Every region deals with old gods' resentment in its own way: Liyue has the Yakshas against the monsters born from the remains, Inazuma has the Sacred Sakura that must be periodically cleansed, Sumeru has Forest Rangers to watch the Withering, and Natlan held the Pilgrimage of the Return of the Sacred Flame to produce Contending Fire against the Abyss.
- Gods can be raised from lesser beings by another god's gift. Boreas, a wolf from Snezhnaya, was made a god by Koitar's blessing, and Barbatos began as a wind spirit.

Archon war: Gods ruled Teyvat before the Archon War. When the Heavenly Principles' functions were ruined in the war of funerary flame, a new world order was arranged and seven divine seats opened in Celestia. The continent then fell into a long series of conflicts that ended about 2,000 years ago. The war allegedly began over those seats, which may coincide with the creation of the Gnoses. Scholars believe Celestia started the war and set its rules. Of the combatants, only seven victors remained; they became The Seven, each with a Gnosis and a share of an elemental Authority from the Seven Sovereigns.

Each region's war looked different:
- Mondstadt: about 2,600 years ago the wolf-god Boreas and the God of Storms, Decarabian, fought to a stalemate, until Decarabian's people overthrew him. Barbatos became Archon; Boreas judged himself unfit for the seat and withdrew, and later chose to pass on, letting his power flow into the land.
- Liyue: the Guili Assembly founded by Guizhong, Rex Lapis and Marchosius was destroyed in the chaos about 3,700 years ago. Rex Lapis gathered the survivors and founded Liyue Harbor south of Mt. Tianheng, and subdued gods and monsters such as Osial, Chi and the Mistress of Chenyu Vale. Havria was murdered by her people, and the survivors of Sal Terrae scattered across Liyue.
- Inazuma: the twin gods Makoto and Ei won. Makoto became Electro Archon with Ei as her kagemusha. The only slain rival god known is Orobashi of Watatsumi Island, and Ei rather than Makoto did the killing.
- Sumeru: King Deshret, Nabu Malikata and Greater Lord Rukkhadevata allied in Ay-Khanoum rather than fighting each other, though Deshret still fought other gods such as Remus, Heryshaf, Sobek and Thoth. Nabu Malikata was corrupted by the Abyss; the alliance broke and Rukkhadevata left.
- Fontaine: Remus was the only god on the surface, because Egeria was held beneath the waves at the Heavenly Principles' bidding. After Remus died at the hands of Phobos and Remuria drowned, Egeria was freed and made Archon.
- Natlan: gods had no place. Dragons and humans fought, and the first Pyro Archon was the human Xbalanque, who defeated the Sovereign Xiuhcoatl and was ascended by Ronova.

Dark sea: Gods who would not live under The Seven fled to islands in the Dark Sea, outside The Seven's control, and became evil gods (according to the aerosiderite item text). Dark Sea details belong to the Dark Sea entry.

Gods by kind: The word "god" covers several groups.
- The Seven Archons, the victors who preside over the seven nations, each bound to an element and an ideal.
- Older gods, some dead, sealed or in changed form. The wiki lists Bennu, Shesepankh, Heryshaf, Sobek and Thoth, Bifrons, Boreas, Chi, Decarabian, Guizhong, Havria, Marchosius (now Guoba), Orobashi, Osial, Remus, Tao Dou and King Deshret, along with many unnamed gods known only from remains, tombs or quest mentions.
- The Moon Goddesses, created by Nibelung in the dragons' era and later folded into the Heavenly Principles' order, so people call them gods.
- Angels, the Heavenly Principles' former envoys, are not gods in the strict sense per Nicole, but some individuals are called gods.

Celestia relationship: Celestia is the gods' realm and the seat of the Heavenly Principles and the Four Shades, though several gods have shown wariness or resentment toward it. Archons resonate with Celestia through their Gnoses, and each holds a divine seat there. Celestia monitors events in Teyvat and can issue directives to the Four Shades. In the 7.1 Archon Quest Black Feathers Scattered at Parting, Rhinedottir says Celestia detected the incident and a directive in her mind demands she use her Authority to rectify Ronova's mistake; Celestia reclaims Ronova's Authority of Death as punishment, and Rhinedottir says it is now watching her and Naberius closely.

Accounts: - Scholars in Teyvat believe Celestia launched the Archon War and set its rules.
- Mondstadt tradition credits Barbatos with becoming Archon after the rebellion against Decarabian; Boreas's side, told in item text (Boreal Wolf's Nostalgia), is that he judged himself unworthy of the seat, and Varka's Story Quest (6.4) adds that he went back to Nod-Krai and slept.
- Venti and Nahida disagree on what an Archon's power depends on (control of the nation versus the people's faith).
- Scholars concluded from the Vision Hunt Decree year that the Archons' will plays a role in granting Visions; Raiden Shogun is surprised by this and rejects their conclusion.
- The English text calls The Seven "Archons" while older gods are just "gods"; early localisation used "archon" loosely, and the Chinese text has no equivalent word.

Open questions: Canon does not state how godhood is conferred in general, whether the nations' territories were set before the Archon War, how many gods remain in Celestia, or what exactly happened to many unnamed gods known only through remains. Do not resolve these in scene; treat them as unknown.

How {{char}} behaves: In narration, treat gods as individuals with personal histories, not a uniform class. Their death and remains are dangerous: expect curses, resentment and monsters around old divine remains. Mortals in Teyvat mostly know gods through nation-specific legend and may not know that a bard or scholar is a god.

Connections: Related entries: The Seven, Celestia, Heavenly Principles, Gnosis, Seven Sovereigns, the Archon War, the Dark Sea, Four Shades, Angels and the Three Moons.

84.content: Dead gods leave power and obsession behind. A god killed against their will can poison the land, as Havria's death salinized her murderers, or leave curses of death, disease and madness. Remains can be sealed or neutralised: the Harvisptokhm, the Narukami Pillars, Liyue's Yakshas, Inazuma's Sacred Sakura. Injected into a human, remains can drive them mad, change their personality or grant unusual power.

85.comment: God: Chosen death of a god
85.content: A god who dies by choice can release their power in a controlled way, leaving no harmful effects. Boreas and Marchosius did so. Remus's death likewise caused no corruption, and his will preserved Capitolium. Marchosius's power went to the land and lives on as Guoba.

86.content: Venti told the Traveler that Vision holders are "allogenes" who may one day ascend to godhood. Mortals who accomplish great heroic deeds are said to ascend to Celestia. Raiden Shogun was surprised to hear that scholars connected the Vision Hunt Decree with the lack of new Electro Visions.

87.content: A wolf from Snezhnaya raised to godhood by Koitar's blessing. He fought Decarabian to a stalemate in Old Mondstadt and, after Decarabian fell, judged himself unworthy of the Anemo seat. Per Varka's Story Quest (6.4), he returned to the Royal Court of the Seelie in Nod-Krai and slept for a thousand years, then split his soul to travel to Mondstadt, where he let his physical body die and his power flow into the ley lines. His spirit remains as the North Wind over Wolvendom; in 6.4 the part of him left in Nod-Krai, corrupted, also chose to return its power to the ley lines.

88.content:
Heavenly Principles (also: Phanes, Primordial One, First Descender, Great Ruler of the Firmament, First Usurper, Pitkamoonen, Lord of the Seven Calamities): The Heavenly Principles is the god who rules Teyvat from Celestia: the First Descender, a being from the sea of stars beyond the false sky. It conquered the dragon Sovereigns, remade the world, created humanity, and governs through "laws" enforced by its four Shades, the Archons' thrones and the Gnoses. Before Sun and Moon calls it the Primordial One and suggests the name Phanes. It has slept since the Cataclysm 500 years ago, but Celestia still acts in its name.

Ordinary people know only a distant heaven. Dragons and rebels call it a tyrant or usurper, and the Tsaritsa's Fatui, the Abyss Order and the Traveler's sibling all work toward opposing it.

Established: It made four Shades, copies of itself: Naberius (Life), Ronova (Death), Istaroth (Time), Asmoday (Space). It took the Sovereigns' Authorities, which became the Archons' Authorities, and it enclosed Teyvat under the false sky. About 6,000 years ago it defeated the dragon king Nibelung in the War of Funerary Flame but was badly wounded.

Celestial nails punish lands that defy or test its order. It distrusts forbidden knowledge, the Abyss and beings who seek power beyond their station. It edits the world's records through Irminsul. Descenders stand outside its laws, and Irminsul does not record them.

- It used Phlogiston, Teyvat's primordial energy, as the basis for modern elemental energy, split like light into seven colours, to develop a power better suited to countering the Abyss (Lord of the Night, Natlan Archon Quest, 5.1).
- Apep says Irminsul existed before the Heavenly Principles arrived. The Heavenly Principles "usurped and refashioned" it to serve humanity and to anchor the world's fate.
- Its curses act on fate itself. In 7.1, Ronova's curse of immortality on Khaenri'ahns outlasted the loss of her Authority because the Heavenly Principles had authorised it. Her curse of death on Snezhnaya ended with her Authority because the Heavenly Principles never sanctioned it.

Nature: It is said to be winged, crowned and androgynous, of "gender unknowable". It is absolutist: it loves humanity on its own terms and strikes hard at threats to its order.

The moon goddess Canon (Frost Moon) said it held an "almost paranoid hostility" toward lifeforms seeking power, or perhaps feared them. Rhinedottir says it has "a deep love for humanity", so killing humans without its approval is a grave sin. The Frostmoon Scions' old hymn calls it "Father of All and Mother of the Gods" and says no one dares speak its name. Neuvillette sneers that the world is ruled under "a cluster of filthy feathers", and he and Jakob both call it a pheasant. Rhinedottir says it had "zero tolerance" for uncertain variables. Yet it forbids its servants to kill the Traveler outright, and Ronova admits she does not know what it values in Descenders.

History: It conquered the dragons, rebuilt the world and created humans, who lived in a unified civilisation under the heavens. After winning the War of Funerary Flame it cast down the celestial nails and set up the Gnoses and seven thrones. It slept after the Cataclysm.

Before Sun and Moon dates the conquest to forty years and the creation of life and humans, with the Shade Naberius, to four hundred years after it. Humans made a covenant with it, and their one taboo was temptation. In the war it shattered the Eternal and Iridescent Moons and flung the Frost Moon beyond the sky. Its nails devastated Sal Vindagnyr, Hyperborea and Lang-Gan, and it banned the history before the war.

- Arrival: the moon goddesses, who kept Teyvat running for Nibelung, at first lived alongside it "like a guest". They slowly realised it meant to dominate the world. Aria and Canon waited to judge its order, while Sonnet opposed it from the start (The First Sliver of Moonlight, 6.3).
- Wounds: Neuvillette's Vision text says the war "ruined" its functions, so it could no longer suppress the world's original order alone.
- Archon War (about 6,000 to 2,000 years ago): gods fought over the seven thrones of its new order.
- Fontaine: Egeria turned Oceanids into humans without its permission. Its judgement became the Prophecy of Fontaine (4.2).
- Cataclysm: it sent The Seven (except Rukkhadevata) and the Shades to Khaenri'ah. On its judgement, Ronova cursed pure-blooded Khaenri'ahns with immortality. The wiki's reading of the 6.3 Archon Quest says it also hid the twins' spaceship on the Frost Moon, beyond the false sky.

Saarelainens bargain: Revealed in 7.1: the Heavenly Principles erased Anastasya's existence for opening a gate to the Abyss.
